- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–2% for next period.
- When sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) or neutral (0.00), model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–2% to account for mean reversion.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > true by >3%), model frequently overcorrects; apply a “lag correction” — reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% in next 2–3 periods.
- If sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish mid-horizon, model often fails to adjust; apply a “sentiment pivot” rule — reduce forecast slope by 10–20% in subsequent periods.
- For 30-day forecasts, model consistently overestimates in early periods (1–5 days) when sentiment is positive; apply a “first-day bias” correction — subtract 0.5–1.5% from forecast day 1.
- If true outcome deviates >5% from model in first 3 days, assume model is “overconfident” — apply a “reversion penalty” — reduce forecast by 1–2% for days 4–7.
- When sentiment history shows repeated “bullish → bearish” transitions, model tends to lag; apply a “sentiment lag” rule — forecast should align with sentiment shift within 3–5 days, not 7+.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, model often fails to capture mean reversion after 15–20 days; apply a “mean reversion cap” — cap forecast at 1.5–2.0% below recent 10-day average if sentiment is neutral or bearish.
